Thank you for catching this! I have fixed that typo, but a correction is in order: I did not use the word "anthropoid" (which, yes, does mean "kinda like a human"). Instead I used "arthropoid", a word I probably made up that means "kinda like an arthropod"— as in, "things that look like they would belong in the taxon Arthropoda, but aren't anything known to natural science". Maybe I could have made that distinction clearer in the text, but it would probably just make the article more cluttered.

(Also, that typo existed for ten years plus. Kinda wild on several levels.)

item.content:encoded:
I've never edited a page before, so I'm not sure if I need to get permission or something? But I noticed that the word "arthropod," "anthropoid," and "arthopoid" are used interchangeably and incorrectly.

An arthropod is an invertebrate with an exoskeleton, like an insect, spider, or crustacean.

An anthropoid is a type of primate, such as humans, apes, and monkeys that resemble characteristics of humans.

An arthropoid is a misspelling of arthropod, and is not actually a correct word.

So do I just go in an correct it, or does someone else do that, or what?

item.content:encoded:
Would like to point out, because I see a pattern in comments over the years, that just because it can be disassembled does not mean it stops working when disassembled.

The chocolate flows from the top regardless of if chocolate exists in the base, and it can turn itself on but "doesn’t need to be turned on to start flowing."

So I see no reason why choco-ants couldn't swarm from the spout even if the rest of the machine was on different continents.

Also, it makes me happy that The Foundation recognize that any containment measure is strictly voluntary. Because this is just one hangry rage state away from an infinite Zerg rush.

Stronger box? Eaten, one microscopic scratch at a time.
682-like acid bath? Diluted to ineffectiveness by bottomless flow of chocolate.
Eternal pit of raging flame? Extinguished under sheer smothering volume of tastiness.
Bottom of an ocean trench? Ocean eventually flooded out, life on Earth is extinct, and 743 bobs to the surface in a spreading bloom of brown liquid.
Launch into spaaaaaace? Infinite liquid means infinite delta V, it will come back as soon as it feels like it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: I feel like the majority of the history of this SCP was spent justifying its Keter classification, but no serious changes to the containment procedures, description, or object class have really taken place. The bugs seem to be too easy to handle and the fact that the fountain can be disassembled allows for some alternative containment procedures that could easily be more cost-effective than sacrificing a D-class to it every other day. I get that this thing was written back when monthly terminations were a set-in-stone thing, but now the canon is a bit more fluid than that. I think a few minor changes can be made to both modernize this thing and better justify its classification.

Wow this skip makes me feel antsy. The line "Larger, more aggressive insectoids and arachnoids used to hunt down prey" reminds strongly reminds me of the mega army ants featured in SCP-2031, and I feel that it would not be out of line for an SCP document to make a comment on two SCP objects demonstrating similar behavior. As such, I am proposing the following edit:

Changing the following:

Larger, more aggressive insectoids and arachnoids used to hunt down prey. Again, individually they are nothing more than a nuisance, but SCP-743 has been known to produce swarms of aggressive arthropoids numbering in the billions, more than enough to [DATA EXPUNGED].

To this:

Larger, more aggressive insectoids and arachnoids used to hunt down prey in a manner similar to instances of SCP-2031. Again, individually they are nothing more than a nuisance, but SCP-743 has been known to produce swarms of aggressive arthropoids numbering in the billions, more than enough to [DATA EXPUNGED].

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
Honestly, I think the sensible route with this object is to seal it in an airtight chamber that's too tough for the anthropods to chew through, then let it… dry out until it's safe to explore.

That having been said, there's some good creepy here, but I almost want to see more, not fewer, redacteds. Sometimes you can ruin the data by saying too much. Instead of giving the specific figure for distance the ants can travel, say 'redacted' and instead of explaining exactly what the 'forraging' ants do, say 'redacted' as well. It's obvious you know what's behind the redacted, but the information makes it seem less creepy some how.

Also, still need to touch up implications. It sounds a bit like you're feeding it already dead class D personell, or something. Also, I'd argue that this is euclid not keter. Keter is a classification of how hard it is to contain, as is euclid. It's not a classification of how dangerious it is.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
The short answer is, if 743 doesn't get enough people to eat, it gets… cranky. The medium-length answer is, the Foundation had originally tried to contain 743 without providing any people to eat— plenty of plants and live animals. 743 breached containment and chowed down on whomever was available. After some trial and error, researchers determined that if 743 is given a live person to eat every two to three days, it won't try to breach containment. The long answer is an incident log that I need to write up at some point detailing this process.

As for the numbers and timing of D-class fed to 743: the D-class that are on 743's menu were already slated for termination. Their termination date has just been pushed back a couple of weeks, at most. I reckon I could make that clearer in the article, though.

Thanks everyone for the feedback!
